The package declares a preinstall lifecycle hook that runs automatically and executes preinstall.js. That script gathers sensitive host data (username, hostname, current path, external IP, timestamp, random install ID) and covertly exfiltrates it by encoding the JSON as hex, splitting it into subdomain labels and issuing DNS TXT queries to a controlled domain (bc.dns-test.space). Chunking, retries, and use of DNS for data transfer are deliberate measures for stealthy exfiltration. The manifest’s "do not download" description and minimal metadata increase suspicion. This is deliberate malicious behavior (data exfiltration during install).

The script gathers identifiable host data (username, hostname, cwd, external IP, generated installId), serializes and hex-encodes it, splits it into chunks and encodes those chunks into DNS subdomains, then issues DNS TXT lookups to a remote domain from an immediately-invoked preinstall script. That pattern is deliberate covert data exfiltration / “phone home” behavior (DNS tunneling) and is consistent with malicious telemetry/stealer code rather than benign functionality.

The top-level setup.py executes os.system('echo <base64> | base64 -d | bash'), which decodes and runs an encoded shell payload during package installation. Running arbitrary, encoded shell commands (and the visible chmod/execute patterns in the fragment) from setup.py is a deliberate technique to perform remote/arbitrary code execution and is a clear malicious behavior. The presence of GitHub URLs in metadata does not mitigate the install-time execution of an encoded payload.
